prompt: What is a partition of a Kafka topic?

choices.text: A log of its own, with offsets that start at 0
choices.why: Right. A topic of three partitions is three logs under one name.

choices.text: A copy of the whole topic kept on another node for safety
choices.why: That is a replica, which lesson 5 covers. A partition holds a share of the messages, not all of them.

choices.text: A time range of the topic, such as one day of messages
choices.why: Time ranges are closer to segments, and they live inside a partition.

choices.text: A filter that a consumer applies when reading
choices.why: Partitions are how the data is stored, decided when it is written.

prompt: Two sales of sales are at offset 40 of partition 0 and offset 12 of partition 2. Which was written first?

choices.text: The one at offset 12, because its offset is smaller
choices.why: Offsets are counted per partition; comparing them across partitions compares two unrelated counters.

choices.text: The one at offset 40, because partition 0 is read first
choices.why: No partition is read first; they are read side by side.

choices.text: The offsets do not say
choices.why: Right. Kafka keeps no order between partitions.

choices.text: Both at once, since offsets are assigned by one clock for the whole topic
choices.why: There is no topic-wide counter or clock; each partition has its own.

prompt: In kafka-topics.sh --describe, what does the Leader column say about a partition?

choices.text: The node that takes its writes and serves its reads
choices.why: Right. With one node, node 1 leads everything.

choices.text: The consumer reading it at the moment
choices.why: The describe output is about storage; consumers appear in the consumer-groups tool.

choices.text: The producer that wrote most of its messages
choices.why: Kafka does not track producers per partition in that column.

choices.text: The partition that holds the most recent message of the topic
choices.why: Leader is a node id, not a partition, and there is no most recent across partitions.

prompt: Who decides which partition a keyed message goes to?

choices.text: The broker, when the message arrives
choices.why: The broker stores the message in the partition the producer named.

choices.text: The consumer group, when it reads
choices.why: By then the message is long stored; reading moves nothing.

choices.text: The controller, which balances the partitions
choices.why: The controller keeps the cluster's metadata; it does not route messages.

choices.text: The producer's client library, by hashing the key
choices.why: Right. The partitioner runs in the client, before the message is sent.

prompt: keys.py with its default settings and Kafka's console producer each sent the key recife to the three-partition topic shops. What happened?

choices.text: They chose different partitions
choices.why: Right. The Python client's default hash is not Java's murmur2.

choices.text: They chose the same partition, because a key always hashes to one place
choices.why: Always to one place for one hash function; these are two.

choices.text: The broker moved the Java message to match the first one
choices.why: The broker never moves messages between partitions.

choices.text: The console producer refused, because the key was already taken by another client
choices.why: Keys are not reserved; any producer may send any key.

prompt: A Java service and a Python service both write stock changes keyed by book to one topic. What is the risk, and the fix?

choices.text: No risk: the broker sorts each key into one partition
choices.why: The broker stores what each client chose, and the two choose differently.

choices.text: One book's changes land in two partitions with no order between them; set partitioner to murmur2_random in the Python client
choices.why: Right. Then both clients hash the same way.

choices.text: Messages are lost; give every message a unique key
choices.why: Nothing is lost, and unique keys would give up order per book altogether.

choices.text: Duplicates; send without keys
choices.why: Different partitions do not duplicate anything, and no key means no order at all.

prompt: The setting that makes librdkafka hash keys the way the Java client does is partitioner=___ .
hint: The name of Java's hash, with _random after it.

prompt: kafka-get-offsets.sh prints sales:1:789 with no --time option. What is 789?

choices.text: The offset of the last message in partition 1
choices.why: The last message is at 788; 789 is where the next one goes.

choices.text: The offset the next message in partition 1 will get
choices.why: Right. The log-end offset.

choices.text: The number of messages consumers have read from partition 1 since the topic was created
choices.why: The tool reads the log, not what anybody has read.

choices.text: The size of partition 1 in kilobytes
choices.why: It is an offset, a count of positions, not a size.

prompt: After a thousand sales from tills.py, partition 2 of sales had none. Why?

choices.text: Partition 2 was offline
choices.why: A partition with no leader would have caused errors, not silence.

choices.text: tills.py writes only to the first two partitions
choices.why: tills.py names no partition; it gives a key and lets the partitioner choose.

choices.text: None of the five shop keys hashes to it
choices.why: Right. Five keys over three partitions, and two partitions took all five.

choices.text: Retention deleted them before the command ran
choices.why: Nothing was deleted: the earliest offsets were all 0.

prompt: A partition's earliest offset is 7513 and its log-end offset is 20000. How many messages does it hold now, with no compaction?
What is the name of a segment file like 00000000000000007513.log?

choices.text: The time the segment was created
choices.why: The time is inside, in the .timeindex; the name is an offset.

choices.text: The offset of the first message in it
choices.why: Right. The base offset, padded to twenty digits.

choices.text: The number of bytes written before it was opened
choices.why: Bytes are positions inside a file, kept in the .index.

choices.text: A random id the broker gave it to avoid clashes on disk
choices.why: Nothing random: two runs of the same data give the same names.

prompt: Why does a segment have an .index beside its .log?

choices.text: To list which consumers have read which messages, and when each of them read them
choices.why: The log knows nothing of its readers; their places are stored elsewhere.

choices.text: To keep a second copy of every key in case the log file is damaged on disk
choices.why: Copies are replicas on other nodes; the index holds positions, not keys.

choices.text: To sort the messages by key
choices.why: Messages stay in the order they were written; nothing sorts them.

choices.text: To find the byte position of an offset without reading the log from its start
choices.why: Right. minilog.py had to count every line; Kafka looks up the nearest entry.

prompt: kafka-dump-log.sh shows a batch line with count: 150 before the messages. What does it tell you about how they arrived?

choices.text: The producer sent 150 messages in one batch, stored as written
choices.why: Right. The broker stores the producer's batch whole; lesson 4 changes its size.

choices.text: 150 consumers have read them
choices.why: The log does not record readers.

choices.text: The broker waited for 150 messages before writing anything to disk
choices.why: The grouping comes from the producer, not from the broker waiting.

choices.text: The segment is full after 150 messages
choices.why: A segment closes by size or age, and holds many batches.

prompt: What does retention delete?

choices.text: Messages that every consumer group has read
choices.why: Retention ignores readers entirely.

choices.text: Single messages older than retention.ms
choices.why: It never deletes one message; it deletes the segment once all of it is past the limit.

choices.text: Whole closed segments, oldest first
choices.why: Right. And never the active segment.

choices.text: The oldest value of each key
choices.why: That is closer to compaction, the next section.

prompt: old-sales had segments starting at offsets 0, 7513 and 14965. Retention deleted the first segment. What did kafka-get-offsets.sh --time earliest print as the offset?
You set retention.bytes on a topic and nothing is deleted for three minutes. Why?

choices.text: The setting needs a broker restart
choices.why: Topic settings apply without a restart; the check is periodic.

choices.text: The broker checks retention every five minutes
choices.why: Right. log.retention.check.interval.ms is 300000 by default.

choices.text: Retention waits until every consumer has caught up
choices.why: Retention does not look at consumers at all.

choices.text: retention.bytes counts the whole cluster, so the limit is far away
choices.why: It is per partition.

prompt: Put what happens to an old segment under retention in order.
items: the active segment reaches segment.bytes and is closed
a retention check finds the closed segment past the limit
the log start offset moves past it and its files are renamed .deleted
a minute later the files are removed from disk

prompt: Which topic suits cleanup.policy=compact?

choices.text: The current stock of each book, keyed by book
choices.why: Right. A newer value for a key makes the older one useless.

choices.text: Every sale, keyed by shop
choices.why: Each sale is a separate fact; compaction would keep one sale per shop.

choices.text: Clicks on the website, with no key
choices.why: Compaction works per key, and a topic without keys has nothing to compact by.

choices.text: An audit trail that must keep every change for a year
choices.why: Compaction throws away old values, which an audit needs.

prompt: After compaction, the stock topic held offsets 4, 5, 6 and 7. What happened to offsets 0 to 3?

choices.text: They were renumbered, so the message that was at offset 4 is now at offset 0
choices.why: Offsets never change; survivors keep theirs.

choices.text: They moved to another segment, where the cleaner keeps the values it replaced
choices.why: They were removed; nothing moves between segments.

choices.text: They are a hole: their messages were older values of keys written again later
choices.why: Right. bk-01, bk-02 and bk-03 all had later messages.

choices.text: They are still there and the consumer skipped them
choices.why: A consumer from the beginning reads everything stored; they are gone.

prompt: What is a tombstone in a compacted topic?

choices.text: A segment marked for deletion by retention, waiting a minute
choices.why: Those are the .deleted files of retention.

choices.text: The first offset still stored
choices.why: That is the log start offset.

choices.text: A keyed message with no value
choices.why: Right. It says the key is deleted; kept for delete.retention.ms, then removed too.

choices.text: A key that the cleaner could not read and left in place
choices.why: Tombstones are written on purpose by producers.

prompt: A new service reads a compacted stock topic from offset 0 to learn each book's stock. The cleaner has not run for an hour. What must the service do?

choices.text: Nothing: compaction guarantees one message per key
choices.why: It guarantees at least the last one; older ones remain until the cleaner runs.

choices.text: Fold: keep the last value it sees for each key, and drop keys whose last message is a tombstone
choices.why: Right. Uncompacted parts still hold old values, so the reader folds.

choices.text: Wait for the cleaner before reading
choices.why: The active segment is never compacted, so waiting never finishes the job.

choices.text: Read from the log-end offset instead
choices.why: Then it sees only future changes, not the current stock.

prompt: A topic keyed by shop goes from 3 to 4 partitions. What happens to the messages already stored?

choices.text: Kafka rehashes them, moving each to the partition its key now hashes to
choices.why: Nothing already stored moves.

choices.text: They are deleted, and the producers are asked to send them again
choices.why: Nothing is deleted or resent.

choices.text: The change is refused while the topic has data
choices.why: Adding is allowed; it is removing that is refused.

choices.text: They stay put; new messages of some shops go elsewhere
choices.why: Right. A moved key's old and new messages now sit in two partitions.

prompt: Match each change to a topic with what Kafka does.

pairs.right: allowed; some keys move from then on
old segments go at the next check
older values per key go when the cleaner runs

right_distractors: every message is copied to a new topic

prompt: A team wants a topic of customer addresses, keyed by customer, that any new service reads in full, and that does not grow without bound. Which settings?

choices.text: cleanup.policy=delete with retention.ms of seven days
choices.why: A customer who has not moved in a week would vanish from the topic.

choices.text: cleanup.policy=compact, with tombstones for customers who leave
choices.why: Right. The last address per customer stays; deleted customers go.

choices.text: retention.bytes of one mebibyte
choices.why: Old customers would be cut off by size.

choices.text: One partition per customer
choices.why: Partitions are not per key; the hash shares them out, and millions would cost a fortune.

prompt: A topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group of 4 copies of one program. At most how many more copies could join and still each get a partition?
